blocks.text: The king named Artaxerxes is conventionally identified as Artaxerxes I, which would place Nehemiah’s twentieth year around 445/444 BCE. That identification and the exact date remain debated because ancient regnal years and calendars can be reckoned differently. The same caution applies to Nehemiah’s nighttime inspection: Persian-period Jerusalem and Judah are archaeologically attested, but the precise route, locations of the gates, and full line or height of the wall cannot be settled with certainty. Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem are presented as figures whose regional political and kinship interests were affected by Jerusalem’s fortification; the narrative’s conflict should not be treated as a timeless condemnation of later or modern peoples associated with those names.

A related chronological question concerns Ezra: his seventh-year Artaxerxes is most commonly identified as Artaxerxes I and dated to 458/457 BCE, before Nehemiah’s mission. Other identifications and proposals for the order of Ezra and Nehemiah remain debated, so this reconstruction should be held provisionally.

sections.title: Questions of date, place, and opposition

blocks.text: The project announced here becomes a broad rebuilding effort involving households, priests, craftspeople, officials, and workers from nearby areas. It also continues amid ridicule, threats, accusations, and intimidation from Sanballat, Tobiah, Geshem, and their allies. The book’s first-person voice gives this material a memoir-like immediacy, even though the final book also includes third-person narrative, lists, Ezra material, and editorial transitions.
